On the eve of AC Milan’s game against Frosinone, Ruben Amorim spoke to the media at the usual pre-match press conference.

The international break is officially over and Milan will be back in action tomorrow. After wins against Inter and Genoa, the goal is to make it three consecutive wins, although an in-form Frosinone side will be looking to make life difficult for them.

It has been revealed that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Amorim’s strategy appears to be to field an attacking-minded starting eleven, picking up where he left off against Genoa. It’s certainly a bold plan as Frosinone will surely look to cause issues on the counter, as also highlighted by Oliver in his prediction.

Speaking to the media at Milanello, Amorim shared his thoughts on the game, the status of the players after the international break, and the tactical solutions moving forward.

According to recent reports, “We as a club have a big responsibility. Fondazione Milan is really vital because it reflects our values and helps the community. Our doors are always open for everyone. It’s also good for the players to see and live different realities.”.

On those involved in international duty….

According to recent reports, “I think everyone is ready. Of course, we had to control the load during the week, because some of them travelled a lot. I’m really pleased with our players getting game time, because that’s the best way to maintain, so we are ready for the game.”.

On Pavlovic’s status and Frosinone’s style..

“Starting with Pavlovic, he’s doing better. He will be in the squad. I don’t know if he will start or not, so I will see. He wants to play and I want him to play. We miss that fire that he has. Let’s see, but for sure he will be in the team.

“Frosinone are fun to watch, they are the team that runs the most, and we are second so I think we can fight that. They are really good with 1v1s on the flanks. If you watch their games it’s hard to understand their movement. There is some logic in their chaos, but it’s hard to spot.

“They play a different style, more direct, which allows them to have the ball more inside the box. So it’s going to be a really hard game. As I mentioned against Venezia, there are some teams that we need to be really focused against because their styles can cause challenges.”.

Camarda is getting little game time, despite the Ramos struggles. Is a strong deputy striker missing?

“Two different questions. Of course we can say that one more option would be a good thing, but I think the struggles of Ramos are the struggles of the team. We are not reaching the final third, we are one of the worst teams in that sense. So we don’t have a lot of shots.

“I don’t want loads of shots outside the box, because it’s hard to score with those. We need to get into the box and we are not helping Ramos. What I saw against Genoa is that without Ramos, we wouldn’t have scored those goals. But again, we need to do better in the final third, my goal is to push the team forward. That’s my job.

“It’s true that he’s working hard and doing a lot of good. I know that it’s not his sole job to press, we spent a lot of money on a player to score goals, but we are not doing enough to help him. We need to push the team forward.”.

Are you happy with the league standings so far? And against Genoa, you basically played with four attacking players. Can this be a solution for the future?

It has been revealed that “Starting with the last question, it depends on the opponents and the moment of the team. I don’t believe that playing with more attackers means you will reach the final third more. Sometimes you get that effect from having more midfielders, for example. We are always going to change in some matches depending on the opponent.

In a recent development, “On the first question, it’s difficult to say. I think that we have grown as a team quite fast, but I’m not pleased with the overall situation. We need to be so much better and as such, I’m not pleased with where we are in the standings. But of course, I need to say that I’m happy with how the players have worked.”.

During the break, we saw Camarda scoring for the U21s. Could a loan be the right solution?

Recent findings suggest that “I was a young player myself once too. A young player wants everything really badly, which is a good thing. That stated, he needs time to adapt, it’s really hard to play for a club like Milan. You just said there is pressure on Ramos, imagine what it’s like for Camarda.

“I don’t know what will happen in January, but he needs to be focused on these games. Everything can change in just a few weeks.

“I’m really happy with how he has been since he returned from international duty, I heard that Baldini spoke with him at length (as Baldini noted himself), and he returned in a happier mood. I understand the question about January, but January is so far away right now.”.

The feeling is that the team is struggling to keep control at the end of the games….

According to recent reports, “Sometimes even when we are winning, we have dropped the levels in every action of the game. I think we are controlling everything better, you saw it in the second half against Genoa without spending a lot of energy, but I think it’s all connected to the attack.

According to recent reports, “If we don’t create danger when we are leading, we will struggle a bit to kill the games. Of course, we need to address that and we are working on it.”.

On Musah as a left-back and if more versatile players will be signed….

Sources indicate that “That was a specific situation. I don’t know and I’m not going to tell you guys what we are thinking about January. I wanted a right-footed player against Genoa. You saw the runs of Rabiot, so I wanted someone right-footed to pass the ball on immediately.

“Musah is not going to play as a left-back tomorrow, I can tell you that, but it’s an option. I like to have players who can play in several positions.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I think it helps any player to feel the confidence from the club. I think it’s clear that was done with the upcoming contract. Then I also told you when he wasn’t playing that he’s really notable for us. I can tell you today that Pulisic perhaps is the one player we cannot replace.

“The movement in between the lines he brings, we simply don’t have another Pulisic. His absence is always felt a lot, so from that you can understand how notable he is for us. He doesn’t talk a lot, but he lets the pitch do the talking.

“I would put him in the same category as Rabiot. Players who are on another level. I don’t like speaking about individuals, but I think everyone can see this.”.

Can the January transfer window serve to raise the team’s ambition?

Recent findings suggest that “That is the biggest mistake of the substantial clubs. Looking at the table and deciding whether to invest or not. I think the key is to have a long-term proposal. Stick with your plan. We have one and everything is very clear.

In a recent development, “Trying to become a champion by spending money is the biggest mistake. The key is following your plan. I look at the table to evaluate the process as a whole, not to decide whether to spend a lot on signings.”.

Are you keeping track of your players so they don’t stay up late at night playing GTA?

“I will let my friend Gennaro Gattuso respond. Jokes aside, I don’t care.”.

Sources indicate that is a winner a dreamer who never gives up? Are you a dreamer?

“I wouldn’t call it a dream but the goal is to win every game. If you look at my journey, every club I chose, I clearly am a dreamer [laughs]. I really want to be part of this club for the rest of my career, but I also know that I need to prove myself.

“I’m a dreamer, yes, but also very focused on the goal.”.

It’s Andrew A covering for Andrew M, who’s playing hooky again. I suppose after 24 years of writing this blog, a few bad habits are bound to creep in….

It has been revealed that I’m not going to lie, it’s been a difficult week. Fortunately, a lifetime of watching Arsenal has given me plenty of practice at making bad jokes when I don’t know what else to say.

It’s either that or tears, and my eye juice reserves are running low after reading just a fraction of the thousands of messages you sent over the weekend. Bluesky, Reddit, X, Discord, Facebook, Patreon. Wherever I looked, there you were, sending love to Blogs. It was beautiful to see.

In a recent development, and to the handful of you who got in touch with me or people I know because you thought Friday’s revision was about my health, please hold that thought. I’m fine. Touch wood. There are, in fact, two Andrews at Arseblog, and I’m the other one.

Having been crowned the “World’s Youngest Boy” by James on yesterday’s Arsecast Extra, Max Dowman set yet another record last night, becoming England under-21s’ youngest scorer with the winner in a 3-2 victory over France in filthy conditions in Bristol.

It has been revealed that I’d planned to watch from kick-off, but gave up when I realised the game wasn’t on any of the 5,000 channels I pay £150 a month for. Then I saw on social media that Ethan Nwaneri, playing as a number 10, had laid on a couple of goals. So I did the clever thing and googled it. Turns out I needed the official England app and an account. Eyes still rolling, I tried to set up a login, only to find out I already had one. Cue the password reset process, verification codes and me losing the will to live. Just let me watch some fucking children play football in the rain!

Industry observers note that by the time I got the stream, it was nearly half-time. At least that gave me a chance to catch up on Nwaneri’s two assists, both of which were Ozil-esque. First he drove down the left and slipped a neat ball inside for Mikey Moore, at the moment on loan at Cologne, to finish. Then came a teasing dink to the back post that Southampton’s Divin Mubama met first time. Given how little Nwaneri has played for Dortmund lately, it was a welcome reminder of what he can do.

It feels a bit silly to say Max, who was named player of the match, looked comfortable at this level when he’s already got a Premier League winners’ medal next to his GCSE textbooks, but he really did.

According to recent reports, watching him is like reading someone’s really nice handwriting. Even the everyday stuff looks lovely. A touch to bring the ball under control, a little turn, and suddenly the defender who was right up his arse is looking at the back of his shirt. I’ll never get tired of watching him do that.

Industry observers note that as both sides made changes, I expected Lee Carsley to take him off. Instead, he played the full 90 and dug Arsenal teammate Tommy Setford out of a hole. The goalkeeper was at fault for the only goal in Friday’s defeat to Portugal and had another difficult night, spilling a cross into his own net. The rain hardly helped, and the 20-year-old has been doing well on loan at Stevenage, but it was a horrible one to concede.

Industry observers note that when Brest’s Giovani Versini whipped in an equaliser with five minutes left, it looked like England would have to settle for a draw, but Dowman’s tap-in settled it with a minute to spare. Who knows, Dowman and Nwaneri could be on the same pitch again next week when Dortmund visit the Emirates.

Elsewhere, Group 2 of League A of the UEFA Nations League (catchy naming scheme, lads) served up another bonkers evening. Jurrien Timber scored twice in the Netherlands’ 7-0 win over Christos Tzolis’ Greece on Friday, only for the Dutch to lose 5-0 to Kai Havertz’s Germany in Berlin. There were some lovely goals from the Germans – including two from Florian Wirtz – who are finding their feet under Jurgen Klopp. Timber and Havertz both came off midway through the second half, seemingly unscathed. Timber’s pride aside, anyway.

Recent findings suggest that tzolis, meanwhile, was cleared to play after an MRI scan and got through 88 minutes of Greece’s 1-0 win over Serbia. All three sides finished on 11 points, with Germany and the Netherlands going through on goal difference at Greece’s expense.

Tonight, Martin Odegaard’s Norway face Denmark, while Viktor Gyokeres will look to extend his record-breaking scoring run for Sweden away at Poland. Piero Hincapie’s Ecuador take on Bolivia, Big Gabi and Bruno are in Singapore with Brazil, and Cristhian Mosquera and Marli Salmon are in action for Spain under-21s and England under-19s, respectively.

Closer to home, The Athletic ran two Arsenal contract stories in quick succession. James reports that Timber has agreed a upcoming long-term deal, while David Ornstein states Declan Rice’s extension will take him through to 2031. Arsenal already had the option to keep Rice until 2029, so the new deal effectively buys them two more years and gives him a sizeable pay rise for the next four and a half. If he keeps playing as he has been, I can’t imagine many Arsenal fans quibbling with that.

For what it’s worth, we’ve heard on the grapevine that David Raya’s fresh contract is all but done, too, which means the club are making good progress with the lads whose deals expire in 2028, a list that also includes Odegaard, Havertz, Mikel Merino and our two backup keepers.

It has been revealed that there was an interesting discussion on Arsenal Vision’s ‘Friday Night Clive’ podcast about Arsenal elongating their “winning window” while having one eye on the next iteration of the team. If you hand expensive new contracts to players hurtling towards their thirties, you leave yourself financially exposed and potentially blocking pathways for up-and-coming talent. No doubt the club and manager are keenly aware of that. I just wonder how much you can expect the latter to focus on the faraway future when the dynasty he craves has to start in the here and now.

Recent findings suggest that if this week has taught me anything, it’s that there’s something to be remarked for seizing the day. Admittedly, that’s easier when it’s Arsenal’s money I’m volunteering to spend.

If you’re about to part with some of your own (smooth segue, Allen) this year’s Arseblog Christmas Gift Guide is up.

I spent some of last week rounding up Arsenal bits and pieces I’d be happy to find under the tree. Mostly, I wanted to point you towards the independent makers, artists and writers producing stuff I like. In many cases, what I’ve picked is just a small sample of what they do, so have a nose around.

If you’ve got a recommendation of your own, pop the link in the form at the bottom and I’ll take a look.

It has been revealed that right, I’d better crack on with the day job. Lewis is on duty tomorrow and, all being well, Andrew M should be back here before the week is out.

It has been revealed that good morning! I’ve got to say, if I worked at Arsenal and I wasn’t getting a newly introduced contract this international break, I think I’d be taking it pretty personally.

After Monday’s news that both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice have agreed new deals with the club, Tuesday brought the news that fellow 2023 signing David Raya was next in line, swiftly followed by reports that Riccardo Calafiori will also be handed a new deal, and Piero Hincapie will be getting improved terms, too.

Since the end of the 2024-25 season, there have already been new deals for Gabriel, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri, William Saliba, Bukayo Saka, and, of course, Mikel Arteta. With the latest raft of agreements on top of those, that’s a lot of notable people tied down for the next few years.

In a recent development, these deals will mean everyone other than Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Mikel Merino, and Kepa is contracted to the club until at least 2029. That’s a nice feeling, isn’t it? There will be some decisions to be made over a couple of those players and whether it’s time to refresh, you’d imagine, but the bulk of the squad should be staying put and continuing to compete together – with a couple of additions supplementing them, of course – for the next couple of years at least.

Of those four (plus Kepa) mentioned above, you’d have to think Odegaard is the next priority when it comes to renewals, given his importance on and off the pitch and his current form.

I was in a bar here in Berlin catching up with a fellow Arsenal fan yesterday evening (hello, if you’re reading!) and they had Norway’s game in Denmark on. It’s fair to say the skipper continued his fine start to the season.

Recent findings suggest that after Norway went two down against the run of play, Odegaard sprung into action. No player had as many touches on the night, and he was involved in all three Norway goals.

Recent findings suggest that he stole the ball for the goal that made it 2-1, which, by the way, we should have a word for. We have the word equaliser for when it goes to 2-2, but we don’t have a word for the goal that shortens the lead. The Germans call it an Anschlusstor – literally a ‘connecting goal’, the goal that means the scores are now just one apart.

Anyway, Odegaard, pressing as he always does, stole the ball from goalkeeper Mads Hermansen, then selflessly left the tap-in for Erling Haaland. He then scored the equaliser, a goal reminiscent of his opening day strike against Coventry if we’re honest: he didn’t hit it well, he got a bit lucky. But: right place, right time and all that.

And, finally, it was Odegaard’s ferociously whipped in free-kick that struck the hand of Joachim Andersen and allowed Haaland to convert from the penalty spot late into added time. If you’ve got a few minutes, you can see the highlights of his performance here – some of the touches are more than worth your time.

A good night’s work, especially after he was suffering with a stomach bug last week.

It wasn’t just the captain in action yesterday, either. Piero Hincapie played just over an hour for Ecuador overnight, there were assists for Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes as Brazil beat Singapore 7-0 earlier on in the day, and then an assist for Viktor Gyokeres too as Sweden drew with Poland.

Industry observers note that that looks like something he’s clearly worked on – getting his body in the way of the defender and, rather than holding the ball up, looking to direct it towards an oncoming runner. His assist for Declan Rice in Munich obviously looked pretty similar, and it’s not something we saw too much of last season.

In fact, I thought I’d have a quick look, and Gyokeres has 13 key passes (a pass that leads a shot from a team-mate) in the Premier League and Champions League this season. He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions. It’s hard not to conclude that he’s been working on that side of his game, and these Giroud-esque back-to-goal touches for team-mates are more than welcome.

So, plenty of assists this break. Now we just need to harness that at Newcastle on Saturday and actually have someone to stick the ball in the back of the net at the end of those moves. Thankfully – knock on wood – it seems the players have made it through the break unscathed (there was also another behind-closed-doors appearance for William Saliba – a nod to Tom Canton for that story) and should be raring to go.

Lastly, I want to point you towards Arseblog News, where Andrew A wrote something last night on the death of double-winner Peter Storey, one of just eight players to make over 500 appearances for the club. That first double is such an enormous part of our history wouldn’t have happened without Storey’s nerves of steel in the FA Cup semi-final.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you. More the kind where you have three stab wounds in your abdomen and a chunk of your insides taken out. If at all possible, I seriously recommend the former to the latter. Anyway, I’m here right now with coffee and painkillers, which I guess is something akin to Arseblog heritage.

The Interlull is over and that’s it now until March. It’s non-stop Arsenal all the way, and all the focus will be on us and what we can produce on the pitch. For those interested in what our players got up to during this break, and what they delivered for their respective nations, Andrew A has a handy round-up over on Arseblog News. Now it’s about keeping everyone as fit as possible, the manager using the squad in the smartest and most effective way he can, and for some of the players who are capable of producing more doing exactly that.

Sources indicate that I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions [PL & CL].

Recent findings suggest that I think sample size might be a factor here, because when you look at his xG per 90, it’s 0.05 per 90 in both Premier League and Champions League this season, versus .99 and .76 per 90 last season, but obviously he played more minutes last time out. After 14 appearances this season, he’s rustled up a total of 614 minutes; this time last season his first 14 appearances brought him a cumulative 1200+ minutes. The absence of Kai Havertz was a factor, obviously, but it was probably that early season load that contributed to the injury he picked up against Burnley after a solid first half performance.

According to recent reports, the job for Mikel Arteta is to find a way to share those minutes effectively, to have both his strikers scoring and assisting, and to harness some of what Gyokeres has been able to produce for Sweden. It’s often mooted that as a team we need to play to his strengths more, but perhaps these key pass metrics show that the design is more about eliminating some of the weaknesses in his game to make him more effective in the final third for us. Let’s see how it goes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the KMI (Key Match Incident) panel have ruled on the Kai Havertz penalty incident against Hull. They ruled 5-0 that the on-field decision was wrong and that VAR, manned that day by Michael Oliver, should have intervened:.

Recent findings suggest that although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz. Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded.

I get every day is a learning day for ‘ProRef’, the people whose job it is to know the rules of football but week after week seem to demonstrate in new and inventive ways that they don’t. The question for us as fans is, what are we supposed to do with this? Are we supposed to feel better knowing that they’re owning up to mistakes? It feels a bit like getting run over when you have the green light at a pedestrian crossing, a nearby cop just lets the bloke go, but then later a judge notes he should have been stopped and arrested.

Which is all well and good when you’re in a hospital bed in traction with a couple of broken legs and smashed pelvis (I say this only because I remember being in hospital with a bloke who fell under a bus and that’s what happened to him. He was fine though, his mates brought him in loads of joints which he used to share in the smoking room – this was 90s hospital). Which is to say, the damage has been done, the admission the bloke got it wrong in the first place doesn’t really make you feel any better.

From our perspective at least, Martin Odegaard’s winner ensured that decision didn’t turn out to be one which went on to live in infamy – like not drawing the lines for that Brentford goal that time, but it’s still essentially useless. Not least because you just know this weekend or next weekend some other mad thing will happen and they’ll say ‘Oooops! Sorry about that LOL here’s Michael Owen and Howard Webb!’, and some team will lose points because they can’t properly apply the rules of the game to things that happen on the pitch.

Recent findings suggest that finally for today, we’re being linked with a January move for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott. He’s certainly a fine player, but it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me given we already have the best midfield depth in the Premier League, and beyond. Where does he fit with Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Martin Odegaard? Perhaps if, for example, Zubi went there’s a case to be made for a replacement, but as it is he’s struggling for minutes anyway, and you don’t pay that kind of money for someone to come in and be peripheral.

Industry observers note that like most of you, if there’s money to be spent in January, I’d much rather see it go on the forward line where I feel like there’s obvious room for improvement and to increase our depth. The left hand side is the obvious place, it’s hard not to worry about the right a little bit with Bukayo Saka’s injury, and the striker conversation is one which is never quite going to go away. So, on that basis, links to Scott don’t really add up for me. Unless Arteta fancies converting him to another left-back. Then it all clicks, but I think there’s one Bournemouth player we’d all rather see arrive.

In a recent development, right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. In terms of a podcast, I’m not quite feeling up to it today, but what we’ll do is make our Patreon preview podcast free and available to everyone tomorrow afternoon. I should be less sore then, and I continue to be blown away by your many emails and messages. Thank you so much, they mean the world.

Richard Hughes made a lot of mistakes when he was Liverpool's sporting director.

The Englishman spent well over £600 million on new players and, it's still unclear whether their team is any better off.

So, even though Hughes did quite well with some of the deals he made, he obviously had to make a few mistakes on the way.

Right now, Liverpool's entire team could still do with upgrading but, because they have a handful of players who's contract are going to expire in June 2027, they've taken priority.

The January transfer window is now just over a month away so, some transfers are going to have to take place soon, otherwise, the Reds will be left even further behind their title rivals than they at the moment find themselves.

Julian Ward can sign Luka Vuskovic after Richard Hughes chose against it in the summer.

Liverpool's defence has been one of the main areas that Liverpool have tried to strengthen over the last few years.

Virgil van Dijk, Andy Robertson and Joe Gomez are just a few examples of the older players that they were using last season.

And, with Robertson gone and the other two having their contracts expire in June 2027, another defensive rebuild could be on the way.

Many different links with players have emerged recently with Giorgio Scalvini one of them.

However, a recent patch from Florian Plettenberg on Luka Vuskovic's situation is something that should definitely pique the interest of Liverpool and their fanbase.

Industry observers note that "Liverpool have Luka Vuskovic on their shortlist for next summer. The 19 y/o top defender is being monitored regularly," he shared via X.

Sources indicate that "His contract at Brighton is valid until 2031. No release clause will be available next summer. Current price valuation: around €100m (+/-).

In a recent development, "Vuskovic is very happy under Fabian Hürzeler. However, his dream is to join Real Madrid one day.

Liverpool need to sign Luka Vuskovic.

Vuskovic has been a revelation since joining Brighton.

The Croatian had a spectacular season last term while on loan with Hamburger SV with most people thinking that Tottenham would welcome him back with open arms.

However, that didn't end up happening and, instead of keeping the 19-year-old around, Roberto de Zerbi chose to bring Jan Paul Van Hecke through the welcome doors instead.

And, while the Dutchman's performances have been impressive, Vuskovic has probably been the better player.

He's transformed Fabian Hurzeler's defence and, there's no wonder why the Seagulls want a record deal for the centre-back.

Obviously, it's a lot of money to spend on a defender who's only had one season of Premier League experience but, if they did manage to get a deal over the line, Ward would be instantly rectifying a problem that Hughes made for himself.

It would also be a sure-fire way for the Englishman to get fans on his side as, during the summer, most Liverpool fans wanted their club to sign him.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that serie A's sporting judge fined Juventus for holding up the start of the game at Fiorentina, and handed the hosts the same penalty.

  • The rulings came in Official Communiqué No.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that serie A's sporting judge fined Juventus for holding up the start of the game at Fiorentina, and handed the hosts the same penalty. No Juventus player is banned, so Spalletti has a full squad for Venezia, though Bremer and Kolo Muani now have a sanction against their names.

Juventus came out of their trip to Florence with a bill rather than a ban. Serie A sporting judge Gerardo Mastrandrea punished the club for an unjustified delay to the start of the first half at Fiorentina. The hosts were handed an identical penalty for the same hold-up.

The rulings came in Official Communiqué No. 60, published in Milan on 10 November 2026. Mastrandrea reached them at a meeting that day with Stefania Ginesio and AIA referees’ representative Carlo Moretti. The communiqué states that the fines, including those given to individual club members, will be charged to each club’s LCA league account.

Industry observers note that only one club paid more than Juventus. Como received the heaviest club fine of the round, €10,000, for delaying the start of the second half by about two minutes. The judge treated that as a repeated offence. Genoa were fined €4,000 and Lazio €3,000.

Recent findings suggest that more notable for Spalletti is what the ruling did not contain. No Juventus player was suspended. Only two players across the league were banned after round 11, according to Corriere dello Sport. They were Parma’s Ndiaye and Frosinone’s Bracaglia, each for one match.

That leaves Spalletti with a full squad for the first game after the international break. He will want every option. The match in Florence, scheduled for Sunday 8 November at 20:45, was assigned to referee Colombo, with Maresca as fourth official and Di Paolo on VAR.

According to recent reports, it ended in a draw that left Juventus seventh on 18 points, Eurosport reported. Fiorentina stayed two points clear of the relegation zone. Spalletti noted afterwards that his side “are not consistent” and sometimes lose their way over very little.

The ruling did leave a mark on four first-team figures. Randal Kolo Muani, Gleison Bremer and Juan Cabal each picked up their first sanction of the season. Spalletti’s assistant Marco Domenichini did too.

Bremer and Kolo Muani are key players for the coach.

It has been revealed that the count has only started, but it will matter as the season goes on. The fine itself is small, and the sporting picture is unchanged.

Juventus host Venezia at the Allianz Stadium on Sunday 22 November at 12:30.

Breaking: Process of Elimination

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through.
  • It has been revealed that arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight.
  • According to recent reports, in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapie are all reportedly on the verge of latest deals, with Riccardo Calafiori’s deal also in the in-tray for Andrea Berta too.

It has been revealed that arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight. Back in the summer of 2021, the club enacted a policy of buying players under 24 years old. I always felt like this was the true year zero of the Arteta project. That always felt like the window that built the foundations.

According to recent reports, in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since. Emile Smith Rowe also signed a new contract and took the number 10 shirt that summer and now he is scratching around for minutes at Fulham.

In a recent development, the summer of 2022 saw the arrivals of Gabriel Jesus and Alex Zinchenko, as well as Fabio Vieira. The former pair briefly elevated Arsenal to a upcoming level before becoming swiftly obsolete. Vieira was a fairly pricey gamble that didn’t pay off. It was the summer of 2023 that truly established Arsenal among England’s elite. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Kai Havertz’s arrivals turned Arsenal from caterpillars to butterflies.

Three of those players are about to sign newly introduced contracts. Curiously, we have little to no reporting on whether Kai Havertz is lined up for a new deal as yet. Arsenal are banking on their well assembled core to deliver more silverware as they enter their peak years (Raya is 31 which feels close to peak age for a goalkeeper).

Sources indicate that undoubtedly, there are some players who will drift away in the coming years. Mikel Merino, Martin Zubimendi and Ben White feel unlikely to get newly introduced Arsenal contracts at this particular moment in time. (Though these things can and do change). Like Havertz, Odegaard’s deal runs until the summer of 2028 and we have yet to hear rumblings of a new deal.

Odegaard and Havertz have negotiated significant fitness challenges over the last two seasons, which probably explains why they have found themselves lower down Berta’s to do list. Timber has had his own physical challenges too, but he is 25. Havertz and Odegaard are 27. Their next contracts will be their last ‘big’ contracts in terms of wages and their resale value will drop to close to zero if Arsenal tie them down. It makes sense for the club to take its time a little more with both players.

Both are also defining attacking and / or creative players in the Arsenal team. At some point, Arteta is going to have to plot an evolution within this core and it feels like that is more likely to happen in the final third of the pitch than within the core of players who operate behind the ball. Behind the ball, Arsenal are absolutely tip top and have some of the most elite players in the world in their positions.

It has been revealed that that is not as true ahead of the ball. Odegaard and Havertz remain, for my money, elite, defining players for Arsenal. For the purposes of this piece; I am going to speculate that Odegaard is going to be offered a fresh contract given his status in the team and because his role is a little more holistic and he doesn’t solely operate in the final third.

Sources indicate that which leaves us with Havertz. I rate Havertz really highly and believe he is integral to Arsenal’s style, he has the technical quality to play one touch football and the physical quality to act as a release valve and hold the ball up. I can’t think of many forwards who offer both sides of the game to such an extent.

There are several Arsenal attackers I would trade in before Havertz. However, the market doesn’t always bend to your will. Arsenal remain a self sustaining club and in the PSR / SCR era, player trading has never been more notable or more voluminous. Keeping money swishing between the cost and revenue columns is a necessity in this environment.

Sources indicate that clearly, the number one impediment to Havertz getting a fresh deal is his fitness. He is still clearly preferred by the manager to Viktor Gyokeres. I have to say I am surprised (a little unpleasantly) at how promptly the tide of opinion has turned against Havertz. The run he went on very recently that saw him score in the Champions League Final, score the goal that clinched the title against Burnley, a critical goal against Chelsea and the winning goal at Anfield seem to have just bought him absolutely no credit within the fan base, which I find a little surprising.

Industry observers note that however, Arsenal need to boost their attacking prowess overall at some point very soon. Like I said, I would consider Havertz a superior player to all of Eze, Gyokeres, Tzolis and Madueke. The squad is well served for numbers in attack; it doesn’t have any gaps in that respect. It has a gap in elite quality.

Sources indicate that the key to boosting that might not be ‘who is the least effective player?’ it might be ‘who is the most saleable?’ Sometimes you do just have to cash in your chips on a player to evolve and move forwards. It doesn’t always have to be because the player is obsolete or not good enough. Arsenal have such numbers in midfield that there also isn’t really a route into the team there for Havertz either.

If someone offered £60-70m for Gyokeres or Eze, I would accept it and give Havertz a latest contract the next day (assuming he does prove his fitness). But I think those scenarios are unlikely. I am not arguing that we have definitely reached the ‘we must sell Kai’ stage and I will reiterate that, at this moment in time, I consider him a very key player who should pretty much always start when fit.

Recent findings suggest that while he isn’t the most prolific finisher as a centre-forward, crucial goals this season against Chelsea and Liverpool demonstrate his worth. The conversation about moving on only becomes live on condition that the money is used to immediately buy an obviously elite attacker- preferably a centre-forward in that case since that is the gap a Havertz departure would leave.

According to recent reports, but I am certain it is a conversation Arteta and Andrea Berta are right now entertaining. Arteta will want to push the level of the team even further and, to fund what that is going to entail, potentially painful sales will have to be made somewhere. The vigour with which the club pursued the sale of Gabriel Martinelli this summer indicates the manager has the stomach for that conversation too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikel Arteta’s press conference takes place early this morning, rather than the typical 1.30pm start time. I woke up a bit later than usual, and there’s part of me that wonders if I should wait for it before doing the blog, but then that would make the blog a lot later than usual and I don’t want to disrupt anybody’s routine. Especially on a Friday.

So, the talking points will come later, if there are any talking points. My guesses on questions today:.

Also, the bloke from Sky Sports will come to the press conference dressed up as a PS5 controller to ask if the manager is concerned about his players staying up all night to to play Grand Theft Auto 6. Hopefully he requires a firmware upgrade before speaking.

In a recent development, so, in the absence of news and stuff to talk about, I thought I’d point you in the direction of some stuff elsewhere. In a week where we’ve been handing out new contracts all over the place, Phil Costa wonders about the future of Kai Havertz and whether new terms might be on offer for him.

It’s an interesting one because I think it’s clear he’s the manager’s first preference from the two strikers he has available to him. If he was forced to drive deep into the woods and leave one tied to a tree, it’d be Viktor Gyokeres left in the dark forest to try and undo his knots and make his way back to civilisation. But reservations about Kai’s fitness are more than understandable, and while this is a player who has scored big goals for this club since his arrival, there are inconsistencies to his game that can be frustrating.

Sources indicate that he turns 28 in June, which is far from over the hill, but it’s then about the cost of a multi-year commitment to a player who, more than likely, you’re probably never going to get much of a return on. Particularly if you have to add to what is already a significant weekly wage packet, even if others will have taken over the mantle of Arsenal’s best-paid player.

My gut feeling is that we’ll probably keep him though, and jokes aside it probably is connected to Gyokeres. The Swedish international feels like the player most expendable of the two in the manager’s mind, and I just can’t really see any scenario when simply Arsenal hang onto both for another season or two, or decide that both can be sold and then replaced at the same time. We sold two left-wingers and a striker this summer and replaced them with one single player, so it’s not as if our track record of augmenting the squad in forward areas would give you much confidence in our ability to undergo sweeping reform.

Industry observers note that thus, some consistency will be necessary, and if push comes to shove, Arteta will sell Gyokeres a hundred times before Havertz once – unless there’s something to do with fitness/injury. The question then is do we renew now, or see where we are next summer? If we add a younger striker to the mix, the benefit of Havertz’s experience isn’t to be underestimated, and then in those final 12 months, if there’s a deal to be done it can be done, and if not, the club have time to consider other options. At that point, he’ll be almost 29, he’ll have options elsewhere if there’s no future at Arsenal.

Of course players want some security when it comes to their contracts and their futures, it might be a case he wants that and that may force the issue one way or the other, but as it stands, it doesn’t seem to be an issue that absolutely has to be a top priority right now (unlike someone like Declan Rice, for example).

Industry observers note that for more good reading this morning, Lewis writes about Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino (the massive lumpy prick), and the challenges they face with their newly introduced clubs. I know I mentioned this on the Arsecast Extra earlier in the week, but I really feel like the latter escapes the scrutiny he deserves for the evil he has perpetrated throughout his career. Manager of Sp*rs, Chelsea and PSG, and now Man Utd, as well as a stint as a national manager during which I thought he thoroughly shamed himself over the Folarin Balogun incident in the World Cup. I know he’s a big mate of Mikel Arteta, but for me he’s up there with the worst of them. A Maroon5 cover of a Phil Collins song brought to life.

According to recent reports, right, I’ll leave it there. As I noted yesterday, we’ll have a preview podcast over on Patreon later on, but in the absence of an Arsecast this week we’ll make it available to everyone for free via the usual podcast channels. That should be out after lunch at some time.

It’s been a difficult place to visit over the years, and we’ve had some unenjoyable encounters – there particularly during Eddie Howe’s tenure. However, Mikel Arteta more or less has a full squad to choose from, and this version of Newcastle under upcoming manager Matthias Jaissle haven’t been at all convincing so far this season.

In terms of the Arsenal team today, Arteta can flip a coin between Ben White and Jurrien Timber, both of whom were on the scoresheet for their countries during the break. William Saliba is back after another behind closed doors appearance to build his fitness, but for a game that’s likely to be intense and physical, I can’t see anything other than Ezri Konsa alongside Gabriel today. He too is likely to feature in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that in midfield there’s no Martin Zubimendi whose unfortunate run of injuries continues with a hamstring strain picked up playing for Spain against England. The form of Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard means they’re first picks, and then it’s about how the manager views Bruno Guimaraes for a game like this. Even if Newcastle haven’t been great, the pantomime villain in midfield adds a layer of spice that is inevitable after his summer move. If he wants to keep the crowd quiet, he could choose Myles Lewis-Skelly, but he paid £75m for this player for a good reason, and I think we’ll see the Brazilian from the start.

Recent findings suggest that he was a hugely crucial player for Newcastle, and while I don’t think his departure was among the most contentious we’ve ever seen, he will be a target for their fans, and perhaps for players who know him – and his temper – very well. You’d hope at 28 he’s mature enough to deal with all that, and I’m sure conversations will have been had about not rising to any bait. Arteta has remarked more than once recently he wants more from this player, where better to give that than his former club?

As for the front three, I think it will be Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke either side of Kai Havertz. The injury news for Bukayo Saka means he’s going to miss another month, at least, so there’s a massive onus on Madueke to continue his recent improved form, but we’ll need him to add end product to the one goal and one assist he’s provided in the league so far. Similarly, Tzolis had a bright-ish start to his Arsenal career, and while the hamstring injury was ill-timed, we need a player who is ostensibly our first choice left winger to start delivering more in terms of assists but especially goals.

Havertz got the winner away to Liverpool, but had frustrating moments at home to Hull. He’s got Viktor Gyokeres on the bench to put some pressure on him, but this front three has some convincing to do and today would be a very good day to produce performances and end product.

Arteta was asked if the atmosphere at St James’ Park isn’t quite what it used to be, because of the way the team has changed and the inconsistent form they’ve suffered so far this campaign. His message was clear:.

Industry observers note that if that’s the case, it will be even more difficult, because they will be even better prepared, they will have even more necessity to do that, and that’s what we expect. We always expect the best version from the opponent. That’s how we have to prepare for the game, and that’s how we’re going to approach it.

So, there’s no chance he’s letting his team think for a second this might be easier because it’s not the same Newcastle that have caused us problems in recent seasons. Nevertheless, he must have looked at this team and some of the challenges they’ve had under their fresh manager and recognised that this is an opportunity to go there with a settled side of his own in good form and come away with all three points.

In a recent development, it is always a challenge there, but this is a mature Arsenal that should be capable of dealing with a team that has just three wins from thirteen games in all competitions this season. You never take anything for granted, but if we can keep the ball in the early stages, get control, and perhaps even an early goal, the ingredients are there for us to make this a winning start to what is a tricky run of games over the coming weeks. Fingers crossed.

In a recent development, right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. #60404. Opinion: Liverpool ready to sign their next Jeremy Jacquet, he's perfect

Opinion: Liverpool ready to sign their next Jeremy Jacquet, he's perfect

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The young Frenchman was brought in for around £55 million with plenty of fans, pundits and journalists all saying that Liverpool had spent too much on a player who'd never played outside of France.
  • The fact that he was only 20 years old didn't help matters much either.
  • However, to the surprise of many, he took becoming a Liverpool player in his stride and has arguably been one of their best performers this term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation at Liverpool.

The young Frenchman was brought in for around £55 million with plenty of fans, pundits and journalists all saying that Liverpool had spent too much on a player who'd never played outside of France.

The fact that he was only 20 years old didn't help matters much either.

However, to the surprise of many, he took becoming a Liverpool player in his stride and has arguably been one of their best performers this term.

He's far better than Ibrahima Konate ever was and, he's still got another decade left as a top-level player.

So, the fact that Liverpool are ready to sign their next version of him is rather exciting.

Liverpool have entered the transfer race for Giorgio Scalvini.

Liverpool's defence may have had a decent chunk of change spent on it over the last couple of years but, there are still a couple of problem areas that they need to fix.

For example, both Kostas Tsimikas and Milos Kerkez have massively underperformed this season.

Every time one of them is played, fans want the other to come back in and take their place.

Obviously, this isn't ideal considering Kerkez was expected to be the Reds' next Andy Robertson.

However, the centre of their defence also has a couple of question marks hanging over it thanks to the undecided futures of Virgil van Dijk and Joe Gomez.

So, Liverpool being linked with Giorgio Scalvini is hardly a surprised, especially with how much potential he has to fulfil.

"Manchester United, Liverpool and Chelsea are positioning themselves to make a possible move for Atalanta defensive star Giorgio Scalvini, with the highly-rated Italian emerging as a major potential transfer target for 2027, TEAMtalk can exclusively reveal," TEAMtalk wrote.

"TEAMtalk understands that a number of English sides are now carrying out detailed work on Scalvini as the possibility of him finally leaving Atalanta gathers momentum.

"Newcastle United are long-term admirers of the Italy international, but the latest interest is coming from Manchester United, Liverpool and Chelsea, who have all been monitoring his development.

"United and Liverpool are both assessing their central defensive options as they consider potential reinforcements, with Scalvini increasingly emerging as a player of interest to their recruitment departments.".

Giorgio Scalvini could become Liverpool's next Jeremy Jacquet.

Scalvini has been linked with an exit from Atalanta for a fair few years now.

Ever since he broke into their first team back in the 2021/22 season, the Italian has been of interest to many different clubs around the globe.

However, now that Liverpool have proven that they're giving youngsters a go in their starting XI with their use of Jacquet and others such as Trey Nyoni, they have more ground to stand on than other clubs.

Of course, Scalvini is a tad older than Jacquet at 22 years old but, since they're both young and have a lot of their careers left to go, it's clear to see why the Italian could become Liverpool's next Jacquet.

He also plays as the right-sided centre-back in a back four so, he'd fit straight into Andoni Iraola's looks if they chose to bring him in.

Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.
  • For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the upcoming coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.
  • Recent findings suggest that this was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the upcoming coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

Recent findings suggest that this was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

Industry observers note that “Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”.

Industry observers note that asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso noted: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

According to recent reports, “We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

According to recent reports, how different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0.

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Recent findings suggest that already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv.

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

Sources indicate that he signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Sources indicate that caicedo rattles the woodwork with a stunning effort! 💥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/CSIM9ogtSp.

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s upcoming home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

Thanks for reading along this afternoon.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

According to recent reports, he told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

It has been revealed that “The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”.

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”.

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and states, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”.

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”.

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that states when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”.

Industry observers note that with Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really notable. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Industry observers note that next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, defenders Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo hurt their hamstrings at Napoli, leaving unbeaten Serie A leaders Lazio short in defence. The setback hits Gattuso's back line just as Juventus return from the break chasing the leaders.

It has been revealed that lazio’s defence has suffered a double blow. Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo were both injured in the 1-1 draw at Napoli. The timing is awkward for the leaders, who resume their league campaign against Lecce on 21 November.

Exact recovery times will only be set once all clinical tests are complete. The early estimate is about 20 days for each player, Sky Sport Italia reported. On that timeline, both miss the home game against Lecce and could return for the trip to Torino on 28 November.

According to recent reports, not every report is that hopeful. Football Italia reported that the pair should miss both the Lecce and Torino games. Under that scenario, they hope to be available again in the first week of December. The match against Atalanta on 6 December is also in doubt.

Recent findings suggest that tavares has been a real attacking outlet this season. He has one goal and four assists in 11 Serie A games. He also has a long record of muscle injuries. Sutalo has made eight league appearances since joining on loan from Ajax on 22 August.

Lazio must now turn to their alternatives. Alfonso Pedraza, who joined from Villarreal in the summer, is the leading option at left-back. He has played 322 minutes across the league and Coppa Italia. Diogo Leite and Doekhi are competing to replace Sutalo in the middle.

According to recent reports, the stand-ins inherit a strong record. Lazio have scored 25 goals and conceded 9 so far. Keeping that defensive record with a reshuffled back line is now Gattuso’s task.

Recent findings suggest that juventus know Lazio’s quality first-hand. Gattuso’s side won 3-0 in Turin earlier this season. That result still weighs on the table. Five wins, three draws and three defeats make up the Juventus record from their opening games.

Grande chiusura di Sutalo, fondamentale.

— S.S.Lazio (@OfficialSSLazio) November 8, 2026.

In a recent development, two missing defenders will not close the gap on their own. They do, however, give Juventus a window in which the leaders are weaker than usual. Any dropped points by Lazio over the coming rounds would only count if Juventus take care of their own fixtures.

Those fixtures follow Lazio’s closely. Como v Juventus is scheduled for Sunday 29 November at 20:45, the day after Lazio’s game against Torino. Further ahead, Lazio’s aim is to have both defenders fit for the Rome derby on 13 December.

Man United chief Omar Berrada distances himself from Man City's Premier League charges - as Enzo Maresca insists his stars are unaffected by guilty verdict

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER and JACK GAUGHAN.
  • Published: 12:41 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 12:46 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada has insisted he was not involved in any wrongdoing at his former club Manchester City – but refused to rule out taking action against them if their appeal fails.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER and JACK GAUGHAN.

Published: 12:41 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 12:46 EST, 20 November 2026.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada has insisted he was not involved in any wrongdoing at his former club Manchester City – but refused to rule out taking action against them if their appeal fails.

In his first sit-down interview in five months, broadcast on Friday, Berrada tackled a range of topics concerning United but his links to City, from whom he joined United in 2024, were also brought up. He worked at the club during some of the period that City were found to have broken Premier League rules.

Back in September, an independent regulatory commission found City guilty of a multitude of charges brought against them by the Premier League, with financial offences ranging between 2009 and 2018.

The scathing verdict determined that City had 'artificially inflated' their revenues and reduced costs through 'disguised funding' schemes such as 'sham' contracts.

Berrada joined City in 2011 before going on to become their chief operating officer in 2016, raising questions over whether he could end up implicated if City – who vehemently contest the charges – fail in their appeal.

According to recent reports, 'I'm not concerned,' Berrada insisted. 'I want to be very clear about this, right. I wasn't involved in any wrongdoings. I wasn't involved in the proceedings; there are no allegations against me, and in that sense there will be no surprises.'.

Asked if United would push for compensation should City's guilty verdict be upheld on appeal, Berrada remained tight-lipped.

Omar Berrada joined Manchester City in 2011... and moved across the city 13 years later.

Berrada has become one of the main sources of anger among United fans who have campaigned against the owners and the board.

Sources indicate that 'I don't want to comment on that because right now it's an ongoing process,' he added. 'When it runs its course we'll take our view of where is our position as Manchester United.'.

Berrada was not used as a witness in the original investigation and there are no allegations directed specifically to the now-United CEO.

City boss Enzo Maresca, meanwhile, insisted that the guilty verdicts handed down to Manchester City for financial chicanery have not affected his players despite three consecutive Premier League defeats.

City fell six points behind defending champions Arsenal in the weeks before this month’s international break amid a slew of individual high-profile errors that led to claims of Maresca’s squad being preoccupied by the uncertainty surrounding the club.

In a recent development, the Premier League have a range of available sanctions to them were City to lose an appeal set for next month. Those would likely result in relegation to the Championship.

But Maresca does not equate that looming doomsday backdrop with a worrying run of form before they face Fulham at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday lunchtime.

In a recent development, ‘I don't think the players are thinking too much about that,’ Maresca noted. ‘If we want to relate the noise with the defeats, look at [Aston] Villa away. We had so many chances, for instance Iliman [Ndiaye] hit the post, or Brighton where the keeper was man of the match.

Enzo Maresca insists his stars are not thinking about the impact of the guilty verdict.

Erling Haaland notes he is 'incredibly' happy to be a City player and tops the Premier League scoring charts with nine so far this campaign.

‘Then [Nottingham] Forest when Erling [Haaland] had the chance to score for 2-2. I don't think the players are focused on the noise. I don't think they are worried about that.’.

Haaland claimed to be ‘incredibly happy’ about being a City player in a defiant interview with Norwegian television earlier in the week, although few others have addressed the problems publicly.

Marc Guehi has previously stated the players are ‘relaxed’, while Phil Foden refused to discuss it when asked.

Maresca has spent the past fortnight analysing City’s ten league matches and has admitted that the team requires more balance after conceding too many goals to turnovers or counter attacks.

‘I was not thinking that we were doing everything well when we were winning games and I'm not thinking that we did everything wrong when we lost games,’ the Italian added.

In a recent development, ‘For me it is the beginning of something long. I think we are attacking well because we are creating chances and overall we are controlling games.

‘There are moments we are not controlling and we have to realise the reasons why and do better. We are conceding goals and most are avoidable from my point of view.’.

There have been occasions – like the first goal at Forest – when City’s building from the back has put them in serious trouble. Josko Gvardiol lost the ball at the City Ground after no midfielder had shown for possession.

Industry observers note that maresca stated: ‘We reviewed things during the break. The idea is to continue to attack in the same way and try to find the balance when we defend or when we are building like what happened for the first goal against Forest.

‘When you are building and you lose the ball in the build-up it's difficult to build with that.’.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 14:12, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 14:12.

Manchester United goalkeeper Altay Bayinidir is reportedly at risk of having his Celta Vigo loan stay terminated in the new year.

Bayinidir was allowed to leave in the summer after Man United recruited Karl Darlow to be Senne Lammens' deputy.

The Turkey international joined Celta on a season-long loan move with the objective of enjoying regular game time.

However, Bayindir has experienced a similar situation to the one he had at Man United, having been forced to play a backup role to Ionut Radu.

Having been overlooked in La Liga and the Europa League, Bayindir's only appearance for Celta came in the recent 5-0 victory over Salamanca in the Copa del Rey.

With Bayindir's playing situation unlikely to change, Faro de Vigo via Sports Witness are reporting that Celta have a massive decision to make over the goalkeeper's loan spell.

The Galician club are assessing the situations of their loan players who lack prominence and are not ruling out the prospect of cutting Bayindir's loan short.

From Man United's perspective, there is no indication they will look to terminate the goalkeeper's loan stint, but it could still end prematurely if Celta or the player express frustration with how the move is panning out.

Bayindir headed out to Galicia after being deemed surplus to requirements under former Man United head coach Michael Carrick.

While Mauricio Pochettino has since replaced Carrick in the Old Trafford dugout, the managerial change is unlikely to affect Bayindir's status at the club.

Even if his current loan switch is cut short, the 28-year-old will likely leave in January in another temporary deal or a permanent transfer.

In truth, it is only a matter of time until Bayindir leaves Old Trafford on a permanent basis, with his contract set to expire in the summer of 2028.

AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a striking gap in debates about artificial intelligence.
  • Industry observers note that in September, the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights published its report on AI regulation.
  • Sources indicate that AI governance requires more than just a declaration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a striking gap in debates about artificial intelligence. Policy bodies and frontier AI laboratories are borrowing the vocabulary of legal constitutions to guide model development and oversight. However, these statements right now don’t include the institutional safeguards that would make such value commitments work.

Industry observers note that in September, the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights published its report on AI regulation. It uses ‘human rights’ more than 100 times in as many pages, but doesn’t discuss which rights should be protected or how. AI firm Anthropic in San Francisco, California, has written a ‘constitution’ for its model Claude. In it, numerous values are listed as the tool’s priorities, including the preservation of user autonomy. Yet some of these values, such as autonomy and well-being, compete with each other, as Anthropic acknowledges. The document does not provide an independent arbiter to adjudicate the conflict, or monitor violations by the AI system.

Sources indicate that AI governance requires more than just a declaration. It requires a system of accountability. Specific institutions should constrain the tools’ influence in accordance with specific fundamental values and hold firms accountable to individuals affected by AI transgressions. Lawyers call this constitutionalism.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

As a scholar of constitutional law, I see parallels between the current debate on AI governance and how national constitutions have been crafted, broken, borrowed and fixed.

It has been revealed that countries’ constitutions have distinct underlying priorities affecting their design. These fall roughly into two historical approaches (C. Skach Int. J. Const. Law 7, 175–181; 2009). One takes liberty as its priority: describing what people are free to do and what the state should not do to interfere. The other focuses on human dignity: noting not what individuals may do, but what cannot be done to them, regardless of the circumstances or whether they have consented to it.

In a recent development, germany’s post-war constitutionalism demonstrates the latter. Its founding document, or basic law, was designed in 1949 to put dignity first and foremost — as both the highest guiding value and a constitutional right, the violation of which is actionable in court. It established an independent federal constitutional court, which citizens can approach directly, that became operational two years later. The choice of this value and the legal institutions to protect it were a response to the atrocities of the Nazi regime, in which people became instruments of state objectives.

In a recent development, frontier AI companies and policymakers should seriously consider using these features of German constitutionalism. When dignity as a constitutional right is violated — by an AI-generated deepfake or by a chatbot that treats a distressed user as just another interaction — the people affected could petition the court directly, and the perpetrator could be stopped and held accountable.

We need a upcoming ethics for a world of AI agents.

We need a fresh ethics for a world of AI agents.
